channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: HIV activism offers a roadmap for tackling weight stigma
item.description: Although HIV and obesity are not mirror images, lessons from the HIV response could accelerate fairer and more effective care for people living with obesity.

item.title: Axonal defects linked to rare form of Parkinson's disease
item.description: A genetic mutation linked to Parkinson's disease produced abnormalities in a subset of nerve cells, offering a clue about the disease's causes, according to a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The findings offer new clues about how the neurodegenerative disorder begins and progresses, said D. James Surmeier, Ph.D., the Nathan Smith Davis professor and chair of neuroscience, who was a co-author of the study.

item.title: Visual tests could indicate cognitive decline—study
item.description: Simple visual tests could be an early indicator of cognitive decline, a precursor to dementia, according to a new study published in the journal Brain Sciences.

item.title: Imaging nerves during surgery without turning down the lights
item.description: Avoiding accidental nerve damage is an important concern in many surgical procedures. Nerves can be difficult to distinguish from surrounding tissue, particularly in complex anatomical regions. Fluorescence-guided surgery could make them easier to see by using fluorescent agents that selectively highlight nerve tissue. But there is a practical obstacle: the fluorescence signal can be weak compared with the bright ambient light of an operating room. Surgeons may therefore need to dim or switch off the room lights during fluorescence imaging, interrupting normal surgical workflow.

item.title: Why do adults get shorter as they age? And how much height do they actually lose?
item.description: When you picture an older person, you may imagine someone shorter and slightly stooped. It's not just your imagination: most of us gradually lose some height as we age.

item.title: Alzheimer's discovery reveals brain cleaning gone wrong
item.description: A gene responsible for compacting trash inside the brain appears to be a key player in Alzheimer's disease, and doctors may be able to target it to better treat or help prevent the devastating condition, new UVA Health research suggests.

item.title: What are biomarkers? How doctors assess health and pooling people's cells reveals new markers—a biologist explains
item.description: A family of five is exposed to the flu virus, but only two of them get sick. A lifelong chain-smoker lives 100 years, while a professional athlete in their prime dies of an unexpected heart attack. A drug fails a clinical trial due to harmful side effects in a subset of patients despite showing good results in others.

item.title: Women may face higher PTSD risk, and biomarker could help predict it
item.description: Research from the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine suggests a specific stress hormone pattern may signal vulnerability to post-traumatic stress disorder—at least in female animal models—and could help explain why women are diagnosed with PTSD at roughly twice the rate of men.

item.title: Chemotherapy for breast cancer linked to accelerated biological aging
item.description: Chemotherapy helps many women survive breast cancer, but new research suggests that chemotherapy may also accelerate biological aging beyond chronological age and increase the risk of earlier death from other causes. The findings point to a need to explore whether interventions to slow or reverse biological aging could improve long-term health for breast cancer survivors.

item.title: Genetic variant among Black people linked to hardening of arteries, Alzheimer's disease
item.description: Rutgers-Newark researchers have discovered that a genetic variant unique to people of African descent heightens the link between so-called "hardening of the arteries" and Alzheimer's disease.

item.title: Study shows awake brain mapping can help optimize deep brain stimulation
item.description: Awake deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery can provide information beyond what imaging alone can capture, helping clinicians personalize electrode placement for patients with essential tremor, according to a Mayo Clinic study published in Operative Neurosurgery.

item.title: Brain's 'cleanup' molecule could aid recovery after stroke
item.description: A naturally occurring molecule that helps the brain clear away damaged blood cells could open the door to new treatments for one of the deadliest forms of stroke, research led by University of Manchester scientists suggests.

item.title: Blood proteins that may predict brain and cardiovascular health issues identified
item.description: Researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), have identified four proteins in the blood that could potentially help identify people at higher risk of worsening cerebrovascular disease, cognitive decline, serious heart- and stroke-related events, and mortality.

item.title: Researchers detect signs of neuronal damage in the earliest stage of Huntington's disease
item.description: Before motor or cognitive impairments appear and before brain volume loss becomes evident, some individuals carrying the genetic mutation that causes Huntington's disease already show signs of neuronal injury. This is demonstrated by a study conducted by the Institut de Recerca Sant Pau (IR Sant Pau), which has detected elevated levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL), a protein that indicates this damage, in individuals classified in the earliest stage of the disease.

item.title: Patient comfort with AI-driven health care hinges on provider oversight
item.description: More than half of patients (56%) are comfortable with artificial intelligence (AI) making diagnosis or treatment decisions when their health care provider can change or override them, but that figure falls to just 9% when AI makes those decisions without provider review, according to new data from the West Health-Gallup Center on Healthcare in America. The nationally representative survey of more than 5,000 U.S. adults found similar patterns in patient comfort with AI used to interpret diagnostic images or make medication decisions.

item.title: Experimental drug eliminates 75% of aggressive pancreatic tumors and enhances immune system memory
item.description: Many solid tumors, including many cancers of the pancreas, breast, colon and lung, protect themselves with a dense wall of scar-like tissue. That wall keeps the immune system's cancer-killing T cells out. It is a major reason why immunotherapy drugs, which have transformed treatment for some patients, help only a minority of people with solid tumors.

item.title: Growing older in Japan: Gender and living arrangements linked to mental health
item.description: As traditional multigenerational households have become less common, increasing numbers of older adults are living alone or with only their spouses. Over the last few decades, Japan has been experiencing two major demographic changes: a rapidly aging population and a shift in how older adults live. These changes have important implications for health and well-being in later life, as living arrangements can shape social support, companionship and caregiving responsibilities.

item.title: People worry most about hormone-disrupting chemicals in food and drink, least in skin products, study finds
item.description: When it comes to hormone-disrupting chemicals, people worry most about what they eat and drink and least about what they put on their skin, according to new research published in Risk Analysis.

item.title: Coffee appears to change how the gut functions
item.description: If you drink coffee regularly, it appears to alter not only your gut bacteria but also the physiology of the gut itself. That is the conclusion of a study from the University of Copenhagen, which may help point the way toward better treatments for constipation. The study is published in the journal Gut Microbiology.

item.title: Video-assisted informed consent helps reduce decisional conflict in cancer patients
item.description: For patients undergoing gastric cancer surgery, informed consent (IC) can involve extensive information about surgical methods, complications, risks, benefits and life after treatment. Conventional face-to-face explanations can be difficult to absorb in one sitting and require substantial time from both patients and surgeons. Decisional conflict, the uncertainty people may feel when making a treatment choice, adds to this challenge.

item.title: Research challenges fusion for lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis
item.description: For adults with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least three months, the addition of fusion to decompression is not associated with differential effects at 12 months, according to a study published online in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

item.title: What causes pulmonary fibrosis on a cellular level?
item.description: A new UCLA Health study in mice has identified a new potential trigger for pulmonary fibrosis: lipid dysregulation (a fat imbalance) within alveolar macrophages. These are the immune cells that serve as the first line of defense against pathogens and tissue damage. Under normal conditions, they are essential for the maintenance and repair of the lung's airspaces. However, when these cells suffer from a lipid imbalance, they lose their protective qualities, malfunction and begin actively promoting disease.

item.title: A pillowcase that tracks sleep
item.description: An interdisciplinary team of researchers led by Columbia Engineering Associate Professor Xia Zhou has developed PillowSense, a fabric-based sleep-monitoring system. The novel system uses soft sensors to measure heart rate, breathing rate, body movement and sleep posture through natural contact with the sleeper's neck.

item.title: Researchers identify DNA marker that could predict treatment response in myelodysplastic syndromes
item.description: DNA methylation patterns present at diagnosis could help predict which patients with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) will respond to azacitidine. That's the key finding of a new multicenter study involving researchers at Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

item.title: Observations of NICU rounds reveal focus on fluids over nutrients for premature infants
item.description: During daily rounds in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), physicians need to balance many considerations in their decision-making about nutrition plans for premature infants. Often, instead of discussing how much energy, carbohydrates, fats and protein the baby has received, physicians tend to focus on how much fluid was delivered, according to a study published in Pediatric Research.

item.title: Mapping Deep South counties links higher diabetes rates to poverty and food insecurity
item.description: Counties where residents suffer from higher diabetes rates across the Deep South often also face greater poverty, food insecurity and barriers to health care and physical activity, a new University of Mississippi study reveals.

item.title: Blood RNA signal may reveal ovarian cancer precursors before invasive disease develops
item.description: Hoag researchers have discovered a molecular warning signal in the blood that identifies serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), an early, precancerous stage of high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC). This advance is particularly significant because ovarian cancer is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, after the disease has already spread.

item.title: Severe premenstrual mood disorder has three subtypes, symptom diaries suggest
item.description: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a common mood disorder associated with the menstrual cycle. A new study published in Nature Communications shows that PMDD does not follow any universal pattern and that there are three subtypes with different patterns of symptoms. The hope is that this discovery will lead to more individualized treatment.

item.title: Immune proteins offer new clues to how prostate cancer could be prevented
item.description: A new study led by researchers at Oxford Population Health shows that higher levels of proteins involved in activating and coordinating the immune system were associated with a lower risk of developing prostate cancer. The findings suggest that the body's ability to recognize and respond to abnormal cells may play an important role in the early development of prostate cancer and could point to new approaches for preventing the disease.

item.title: Semaglutide may lower fetal oxygen levels, sheep study suggests
item.description: They're the blockbuster drugs transforming weight loss, helping millions of people to shed unwanted kilograms. But while medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy may also improve women's chances of becoming pregnant, what happens to their unborn babies if they continue to take the drugs during pregnancy?
